reply.title: At the Highest Point of a Vertical Throw
reply.story:
When you toss a ball straight up into the air, it slows down as it climbs, hangs motionless for a fleeting instant at its peak, and then speeds up on its way back down. Watching this, it is easy to wonder what happens at the very top. Since the ball stops moving for a moment, is its velocity zero? Yes. Does that mean its acceleration is also zero?

People often assume that if something is not moving, it cannot be accelerating. After all, acceleration feels like a change in speed, and at the apex, the speed hits zero. But if the acceleration were zero at the top, the ball would stay there floating. Instead, gravity keeps pulling it downward every fraction of a second, whether the ball is moving upward, standing still at the top, or falling back down.

By tracking the velocity and the constant downward pull of gravity side by side, we can see why velocity and acceleration are entirely different quantities. Velocity tells you where the position is heading, while acceleration tells you how that velocity changes. At the apex, velocity passes through zero, but its rate of change—the acceleration due to gravity—remains steady.
reply.cardDescription: Explore how a ball's velocity and acceleration behave during a vertical throw. Even when velocity is $0\text{ m/s}$ at the apex, acceleration remains constant at $-g$.
reply.instructions: Adjust the launch speed and gravity, then press play to observe the motion and the velocity-time plot.
